c.tagline: Kurdistan's capital, ringed around one of the world's oldest citadels.

taxi.fareNote: Most taxis are unmetered - agree the fare in dinars before setting off. Ride-hailing (Careem) has limited coverage, so hailing a street taxi or asking your hotel to call one is the norm.

emergency.note: In the Kurdistan Region 104 reaches the police and 122 the ambulance service; 115 is the fire brigade.

solo.f: Government travel advisory is the main factor (5/100)

avoid.reason: No no-go areas within Erbil itself, but do not travel toward Mosul, Kirkuk, or the disputed territories outside the Kurdistan Region.
Carry your passport for the frequent checkpoints and monitor the news, as regional tensions occasionally flare with little warning.

hood_desc: The historic core wrapped around the UNESCO-listed Erbil Citadel and the bustling Qaysari Bazaar, with Shar (Minare) Park, tea houses, and street food; the sightseeing heart and best base for first-timers.

Erbil's historically Christian quarter to the north, known for its churches, restaurants, and the city's most concentrated nightlife and bars (alcohol is served here); popular with expats and visitors.
A modern commercial spine (also called the 100-Meter road) lined with malls, international restaurants, and high-rise hotels; central, walkable in stretches, and handy for shopping and dining.
A quiet gated residential enclave of Mediterranean-style villas, boutique cafes, and restaurants on the airport side of the city; relaxed and family-friendly, away from the busy centre.
lodging: Ramada by Wyndham Erbil Gulan Street

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash (Iraqi dinars); public buses are few and most trips are by taxi. There is no rechargeable transit card or metro system.
transit.hours: Buses and taxis run roughly 6am-10pm; after that pre-booked or hotel-called taxis are the main option.
transit.note: Public transport is minimal - the ring-road layout radiates out from the Citadel, and most residents and visitors rely on taxis. Traffic is manageable outside rush hour.

bus: Erbil main bus / garage terminal - intercity buses and shared taxis to Duhok, Sulaymaniyah, Kirkuk, Mosul and Baghdad

transit.m: Airport shuttle to the terminal checkpoint, then taxi to the centre (15-20 min)
No public bus or rail link serves the airport

tip.r: Not expected; rounding up or leaving 5-10% for good service in restaurants is appreciated.

food.name: Kurdish kebab
food.desc: Hand-minced lamb or beef kebab pressed onto flat skewers over charcoal, served on naan with grilled tomato, raw onion, sumac and parsley.

places.name: Yassin Kebab
places.note: Legendary bazaar kebab shop in the alleys under the Citadel; widely called the best in town.

places.name: Abu Shahab City
places.note: Large complex near Naz City with a strong Iraqi grill of kebab, tikka and chicken.

places.name: Qaysari Bazaar grill stalls
places.note: Cheap charcoal grills feeding traders all day; sit at a shared table and point.

food.name: Dolma
food.desc: Vine leaves plus hollowed aubergine, onion and pepper stuffed with spiced rice and lamb, stacked in a pot and simmered with tomato and lemon.

places.name: Miran Restaurant
places.note: Best-known dolma address in Erbil; the pot is upended at the table.

places.name: Sufra Restaurant
places.note: Traditional dining room celebrated for Kurdish home cooking, including dolma and tawa Kurdi.

places.name: Qaysari Bazaar lunch canteens
places.note: Home-style trays of dolma sold by weight at midday to bazaar workers.

food.name: Kurdish biryani
food.desc: Not the Indian version: buttery rice with vermicelli, raisins, almonds and peas layered over chicken or lamb and topped with fried potato.

places.name: Altun Saray Restaurant
places.note: Erbil's best-known biryani house; large plates, always busy at lunch.

places.name: Abu Shahab City
places.note: Does a rich biryani alongside its famous quzi sham pastry-topped rice.

places.name: Sufra Restaurant
places.note: Traditional room with a solid biryani for people who want table service.

food.name: Kubba
food.desc: Shells of bulgur or rice dough packed with spiced minced lamb and either fried crisp or dropped into a sour tomato and beetroot broth as kubba hamuth.

places.name: Qaysari Bazaar kubba stalls
places.note: Fried kubba sold hot from trays in the covered market; a proper cheap snack.

places.name: Sufra Restaurant
places.note: Serves the soupy kubba hamuth as well as the fried Mosul-style version.

places.name: Miran Restaurant
places.note: Kubba appears on the traditional mezze spread alongside the dolma.

food.name: Quzi
food.desc: Whole lamb shank or shoulder slow-cooked until falling apart and set over spiced rice with nuts and raisins; the Iraqi celebration dish.

places.name: Abu Shahab City
places.note: Its quzi sham, biryani sealed under a layer of fried pastry, is the house speciality.

places.name: De Fermo Restaurant
places.note: Grill house whose menu runs from shawarma and tikka to a well-regarded quzi.

places.name: Altun Saray Restaurant
places.note: Serves quzi alongside the biryani that made its name.

food.name: Tawa Kurdi
food.desc: Kurdish tray stew of lamb, aubergine, tomato, pepper and okra baked slowly in its own juices and eaten straight from the pan with flatbread.

places.name: Sufra Restaurant
places.note: Celebrated for its traditional ambience and its signature tawa Kurdi.

places.name: Miran Restaurant
places.note: Kurdish home-style tray dishes served family style.

places.name: Qaysari Bazaar lunch canteens
places.note: Daily tray stews spooned out at working-lunch prices.

food.name: Kurdish chai
food.desc: Strong black tea served scalding in a small waisted istikan glass with a sugar cube; ordering one buys you a seat for as long as you like.

places.name: Machko Chaikhana
places.note: Family-run since 1940, built into the Citadel wall; the meeting point for Erbil's writers and journalists.

places.name: Qaysari Bazaar tea houses
places.note: Tea benches wedged between the shops in the 13th-century covered market.

places.name: Shar Garden tea stalls
places.note: Open-air glasses of chai on the main square below the Citadel, busiest at dusk.

food.name: Mastaw
food.desc: Chilled salted yoghurt thinned with water, sometimes with dried mint; the standard cooling partner to grilled meat in the Kurdish summer.

places.name: Yassin Kebab
places.note: Served ice cold in a metal cup with the kebab; the classic pairing.

places.name: Abu Shahab City
places.note: House jugs of mastaw with the grills; also does fresh fruit juices.

places.name: Sufra Restaurant
places.note: Traditional accompaniment to the dolma and tawa dishes.

landmarks: Erbil Citadel
A UNESCO-listed fortified mound claimed as the world's oldest continuously inhabited settlement, rising 30 meters above the city on 6,000 years of history.
Qaysari Bazaar
A labyrinthine covered market at the citadel's foot, piled with spices, gold, carpets and honey, where tea sellers weave between the crowds.
Mudhafaria Minaret (Choli Minaret)
A leaning 36-meter brick minaret from the 12th-century reign of Muzaffar ad-Din Gokburi, the elegant survivor of medieval Erbil.
Shar Park and the Citadel Fountains
The city's grand central plaza below the citadel, where cascading fountains, tea houses and evening crowds make Erbil's liveliest people-watching.
Jalil Khayat Mosque
Erbil's largest mosque, a modern Ottoman-and-Egyptian-inspired masterpiece of domes, twin minarets and dazzling interior calligraphy.
Sami Abdulrahman Park
A vast green lung of lakes, rose gardens and memorials built on a former military base, beloved by picnicking Kurdish families.
Kurdish Textile Museum
A restored citadel mansion showcasing nomadic carpets, costumes and weaving traditions of Kurdistan's tribes, with rooftop views over the old town.
Erbil Civilization Museum
The city's archaeological collection, spanning Sumerian, Assyrian and Abbasid treasures unearthed across one of humanity's oldest urban landscapes.
Khanzad Castle
A stout 16th-century hilltop fortress just north of the city, named for the legendary Kurdish princess who ruled the Soran emirate.
Korek Mountain Resort
A cable-car-served mountain retreat two hours from Erbil, offering alpine views, winter snow and summer escapes above the Rawanduz gorge.

train.note: Erbil has no passenger rail service: the old eastern line from Baghdad towards Kirkuk and Erbil has been out of use for decades and the northern line through Mosul is still under reconstruction. Iraqi Republic Railways currently runs only a limited network centred on Baghdad, mainly the overnight Baghdad-Basra service, with tickets sold at station counters and no online booking. Iraq has had no regular international passenger trains since 2003, so every cross-border arrival in Erbil is by road or air.

intl.to: Diyarbakır, Mardin & Istanbul (Turkey) - via the Habur/Ibrahim Khalil crossing at Zakho, roughly 12 hours from Diyarbakır
intl.op: Turkish intercity coach companies, bookable through obilet

intl.to: Tehran & Urmia (Iran) - via the Piranshahr/Haji Omaran or Bashmaq/Penjwen crossings, about 10 hours and 950 km from Tehran
intl.op: Iranian and Kurdish long-distance coach operators — tickets at the Erbil and Tehran coach terminals

bus.note: Coaches and shared taxis use Erbil's main garages on the ring road rather than a single central terminal, and drivers wait to fill before leaving, so mornings are the reliable time to travel. From Turkey more than five buses a day leave Diyarbakır otogar for Duhok (7-9 hours) and Erbil (about 12 hours), and it is also common to take a shared taxi from Silopi across the Habur bridge to Zakho and change there. The Kurdistan Region issues its own entry stamp on arrival for many nationalities, which is separate from a federal Iraqi visa, and travelling on from Erbil to Baghdad or Kirkuk means passing federal checkpoints - the Baghdad road takes about 5 hours. There is no online booking for Iraqi-side coaches; you pay at the counter or to the driver.

ferry.note: Erbil lies deep inland in northern Iraq, hundreds of kilometres from the sea and with no navigable river link, so there are no ferry or boat services.

full.name: Lalish
full.blurb: Holiest site of the Yazidi faith, a mountain village of conical shrine spires and sacred springs in Iraqi Kurdistan's hills.

full.name: Rawanduz Gorge & Gali Ali Beg Waterfall
full.blurb: Dramatic Kurdish mountain gorge with a roadside waterfall plunging beside the highway toward the Iranian border.

full.name: Akre
full.blurb: Hillside Kurdish town famous for its Newroz fire festival, with old stone houses stacked up a steep mountainside.

full.name: Sulaymaniyah
full.blurb: Kurdistan's cultural capital, home to the Amna Suraka museum on Saddam-era atrocities and a lively covered bazaar.

full.name: Amadiya (Amedi)
full.blurb: Ancient fortified town perched atop a flat-topped mountain plateau, reached by a winding road through Kurdish highlands.
